profiles.title: Load website scripts in the right order
profiles.problem: A calendar widget fails if its script runs before jQuery. Several widgets can request overlapping scripts.
profiles.role: Django merges ordered asset lists with Python TopologicalSorter. Ready items have no unfinished prerequisites: the Kahn source-removal pattern.
profiles.benefit: Preserves required script order and warns when the requested order is cyclic. This is a correctness benefit, not a reported speedup.
profiles.limit: Does not minimize page-load time or replace a browser’s script loader.
profiles.match: Core source-removal mechanism verified through Django and graphlib.
profiles.input: Two widgets require jQuery; both must come before noConflict.
profiles.output: jQuery first, calendar and time in a valid middle order, noConflict last.
profiles.question: Which part would dominate for large asset lists: graph construction, duplicate handling, or ordering?

profiles.title: Finish one image branch before starting another
profiles.problem: Starting every chunk first can keep many intermediate results alive.
profiles.role: The documented local scheduler favors recently ready tasks with a LIFO policy, helping finish existing work.
profiles.benefit: Explains a practical reason to choose a stack rather than a queue among eligible tasks.
profiles.limit: No minimum-memory guarantee; the entire Dask policy includes more than a stack.
profiles.match: Shared ready-stack policy, not a reproduction of every Dask scheduler.
profiles.input: Two independent load → filter → save branches.
profiles.output: A valid order that tends to finish one branch before the other.
profiles.question: When does this policy help data lifetime, and when does it reduce available parallelism?

profiles.title: Choose useful build work first
profiles.problem: Many source files are ready to compile, but some belong to longer remaining build chains.
profiles.role: Ninja compares ready build edges using critical-path weights and an ID tie-break.
profiles.benefit: A concrete use of priority selection inside dependency-respecting execution.
profiles.limit: Priority alone does not establish an optimal build time. Real resource pools and durations matter.
profiles.match: The demo uses fixed illustrative scores, not Ninja’s full priority calculation.
profiles.input: Header generation precedes two compilation tasks; both feed linking and testing.
profiles.output: Only eligible tasks are selected, with the higher supplied priority first.
profiles.question: Can an improvement retain the same decisions while reducing the cost of maintaining the queue?

profiles.title: Produce a repeatable dependency list
profiles.problem: Two valid asset orders can differ just because input enumeration changed.
profiles.role: A lexicographical topological sort chooses a stable key among eligible nodes.
profiles.benefit: Provides a documented algorithm for reproducible dependency-respecting output.
profiles.limit: The website use is an adaptation. No separate production adoption or speedup was verified for this exact policy.
profiles.match: Library algorithm verified; asset-manifest example is illustrative.
profiles.input: The same script dependencies, with task names used as tie-break keys.
profiles.output: A deterministic valid order for this chosen key.
profiles.question: Does the study need identical output, or merely any valid order? That changes its correctness target.

profiles.title: Run a pipeline in dependency stages
profiles.problem: A batch system must know which jobs can start before their results are consumed.
profiles.role: Topological generations expose layers of eligible work; graphlib separately exposes batches of currently ready tasks.
profiles.benefit: Helps visualize parallel opportunities and dependency barriers.
profiles.limit: Strict layers add a barrier; graphlib ready batches need not be executed as synchronous generations.
profiles.match: Exact generation operation in NetworkX; practical dispatch motivation in graphlib.
profiles.input: Two independent image-processing chains.
profiles.output: Loads form one generation, then filters, then saves.
profiles.question: Is waiting for a whole generation necessary, or is it extra delay introduced by the executor?

profiles.title: Apply database updates safely
profiles.problem: A foreign-key update cannot run before both required tables exist.
profiles.role: Django uses iterative DFS to construct forward and backward migration plans.
profiles.benefit: Finds prerequisites before applying a requested migration, and dependents before removing one.
profiles.limit: Real migration graphs may include replaced migrations and target-specific traversal.
profiles.match: DFS family verified. The example visits the whole graph, whereas Django plans around a target.
profiles.input: Create users and posts, add their relationship, then add its index.
profiles.output: A dependency-valid migration sequence, with AddAuthor before AddIndex.
profiles.question: Would a target-specific traversal avoid work that a whole-graph ordering performs unnecessarily?

profiles.title: Explain a possible lock-order problem
profiles.problem: Different code paths acquire locks in conflicting orders and may hang.
profiles.role: Linux lockdep includes breadth-first graph searches in its dependency checks.
profiles.benefit: A graph path can explain the chain connecting one lock class to another.
profiles.limit: Real lock modes and annotations exceed this example; finding a path is not itself proof of an observed deadlock.
profiles.match: BFS routine is present in lockdep; the simplified path example is not a kernel trace.
profiles.input: CacheLock → UserLock → LogLock; ask whether CacheLock reaches LogLock.
profiles.output: The two-edge lock-dependency path.
profiles.question: Can an explanation remain short without silently ignoring relevant dependency types?

profiles.title: Keep an interactive dependency check responsive
profiles.problem: A search may be too expensive to finish within an interactive work budget.
profiles.role: The demonstration limits edge inspections and preserves UNKNOWN when it has not proved an answer.
profiles.benefit: Makes the cost-versus-certainty trade-off explicit.
profiles.limit: No named product was verified to use this exact cutoff rule. A truncated search cannot certify no path.
profiles.match: Related to dependency checks; this particular budgeted procedure is a local teaching mechanism.
profiles.input: The lock path needs two edges; the initial search budget is one.
profiles.output: UNKNOWN, not “no dependency”; increasing the budget finds the path.
profiles.question: Which inexpensive certificate could avoid an unnecessary search while remaining exact?

profiles.title: Remove distracting arrows from a build diagram
profiles.problem: A diagram contains both Compile → Test → Package and an extra Compile → Package arrow.
profiles.role: Transitive reduction removes an edge only when another path preserves its reachability.
profiles.benefit: Graphviz provides a real reduction tool; workflow research uses related dependency removal for cleanup planning.
profiles.limit: Not safe when an edge has extra semantics beyond ordering. Finding redundancy can cost more than processing it.
profiles.match: Graphviz operation is exact; the deployment pipeline and reference implementation are illustrative.
profiles.input: A four-step deployment DAG with three redundant shortcuts.
profiles.output: Three necessary chain edges remain, with the same reachability.
profiles.question: How much work is worth spending to prove that an edge is redundant?

profiles.title: Check all legal orders of a tiny test case
profiles.problem: A new scheduler seems correct on one output, but another valid order may expose a bug or a smaller peak.
profiles.role: Enumerate every valid order of a small DAG and check each against the proposed invariant.
profiles.benefit: Provides an exact local oracle when the graph is tiny.
profiles.limit: Output count can grow factorially. This is a testing use, not a scalable production scheduler.
profiles.match: Documented enumeration function; our test-fixture use is local.
profiles.input: MakeSchema must precede LoadData and BuildIndex.
profiles.output: Exactly two valid orders for the two independent final tasks.
profiles.question: Can a tiny exhaustive counterexample disprove a broad claim before a large experiment is built?

profiles.title: Identify the build chain that limits completion
profiles.problem: Parallel compilation cannot bypass a long chain ending in the final executable.
profiles.role: A reverse dependency traversal computes critical-path priorities; the demo shows longest-path dynamic programming with known toy durations.
profiles.benefit: Explains why critical-path information is useful to a real build tool.
profiles.limit: The 10-unit toy bound assumes enough processors and no extra transfers. It is not a measured Ninja build time.
profiles.match: Critical-path mechanism verified; cost assumptions are simplified.
profiles.input: Header generation 2, UI compile 3, core compile 5, link 2, test 1 time units.
profiles.output: Critical dependency-chain length 10 toy time units.
profiles.question: Are inaccurate duration estimates more important than the cost of computing the ranking?

profiles.title: Recheck a pipeline after a dependency edit
profiles.problem: A user adds a prerequisite after a valid order has already been constructed.
profiles.role: Add the edge and recompute an order, rejecting the graph if a cycle appears.
profiles.benefit: Simple correctness reference for evaluating a genuine incremental method.
profiles.limit: Recomputes unaffected work. Abseil is evidence for the incremental problem, not adoption of this reference routine.
profiles.match: A locally implemented baseline, not a product claim.
profiles.input: Existing lock dependencies plus the new ConfigLock → CacheLock constraint.
profiles.output: A repaired valid order that moves ConfigLock before CacheLock.
profiles.question: How often are edits already consistent with the stored order, requiring no repair?

profiles.title: Catch dangerous lock acquisition orders
profiles.problem: A newly observed lock order may contradict a previously recorded chain.
profiles.role: Abseil explicitly implements Pearce–Kelly ranks and restricted repair for incremental cycle detection.
profiles.benefit: Connects a named research algorithm to a concrete debugging feature in a maintained C++ library.
profiles.limit: Debugging overhead remains; a potential lock-order cycle is not a guaranteed live deadlock.
profiles.match: Named algorithm match verified in pinned source; demo covers core insertion repair only.
profiles.input: A backward but acyclic ConfigLock → CacheLock insertion.
profiles.output: Only the necessary order relationship is repaired; a cyclic alternative is rejected.
profiles.question: Which affected-region shape makes local repair cheaper or more expensive than recomputation?

profiles.title: Group mutually recursive functions
profiles.product: LLVM graph utilities and compiler passes
profiles.problem: Two functions call one another, so treating each as an independent acyclic step is incorrect.
profiles.role: Tarjan SCC groups vertices that can reach one another; LLVM’s generic iterator explicitly uses Tarjan.
profiles.benefit: Lets compiler analyses process cycles as components rather than pretending the call graph is a DAG.
profiles.limit: SCC membership alone does not prove that a function will loop forever or establish a legal task-execution order.
profiles.match: Tarjan utility and CGSCC analysis context verified; the tiny call graph is illustrative.
profiles.input: ParseCfg calls ExpandVar and ExpandVar calls ParseCfg.
profiles.output: One recursive component containing ParseCfg and ExpandVar.
profiles.question: Can a transformation change component boundaries and invalidate cached analysis?

profiles.title: Select the next event or urgent job
profiles.problem: A simulation or job dispatcher repeatedly selects one pending item, sometimes after its priority changes.
profiles.role: Heap queues support inexpensive selection; invalidated entries can be skipped when removed.
profiles.benefit: SimPy documents a time-ordered heap; Python documents changed-priority handling.
profiles.limit: The demo’s max-priority jobs and version stamps are not SimPy’s exact time-based event loop.
profiles.match: Heap usage verified; mutable-priority demonstration is independently written.
profiles.input: Email, Backup and Index jobs; Email becomes more urgent.
profiles.output: Email is selected first; its old stale entry is not executed later.
profiles.question: Do stale entries accumulate enough to outweigh the benefit of avoiding in-place updates?

profiles.title: Check a storage-aware task ordering
profiles.product: XLA scheduling as the practical reference
profiles.problem: A compiler must choose among instructions whose intermediates consume memory.
profiles.role: The local oracle recomputes released bytes minus created bytes for every ready task.
profiles.benefit: Provides a straightforward check of the same simplified score used by the incremental demos.
profiles.limit: This deliberately direct oracle is not the shipped XLA scheduler and is not the strongest runtime baseline.
profiles.match: Score motivation matches XLA; full recomputation is our independent reference.
profiles.input: An image buffer feeds preview and filter tasks before export.
profiles.output: A valid order according to the declared release-minus-production score.
profiles.question: Which oracle checks correctness without becoming an artificially weak performance competitor?

profiles.title: Maintain memory-related scheduling priorities
profiles.problem: Recalculating every ready instruction’s release benefit repeats work after each completed instruction.
profiles.role: The source tracks unfinished uses and revisits affected priorities when one use remains.
profiles.benefit: Verifies that the core update mechanism already has a real compiler application.
profiles.limit: The file model omits aliases and special instructions. These simulations prove no compiler or inference speedup.
profiles.match: Core event mechanism verified, not an exact full XLA reproduction.
profiles.input: Preview and Filter share Pixels and Alpha; the last consumer receives release credit.
profiles.output: The same simplified priority order as full recomputation, with selective updates.
profiles.question: Where is the remaining cost after competent incremental updates are already implemented?

profiles.title: Avoid duplicate bookkeeping for shared image files
profiles.product: Workflow cleanup and compiler metadata context
profiles.problem: Several files have identical consumers, so their remaining-consumer counts move together.
profiles.role: The local example shares counters for equal consumer sets while keeping creation costs separate.
profiles.benefit: Illustrates an exact representation change relevant to data-intensive task graphs.
profiles.limit: No separate deployed system was verified to use this exact grouping rule. Preprocessing may eliminate its runtime benefit.
profiles.match: Related application evidence only; do not present this local variant as a published or novel algorithm.
profiles.input: Pixels and Alpha are both consumed by Preview and Filter.
profiles.output: A shared consumer group with unchanged ready-task score decisions.
profiles.question: Does grouping still help after excluding trivially static final consumers?

profiles.title: Recognize when the last file user is already known
profiles.problem: A file has several users, but dependencies already force one user to finish last.
profiles.role: The local proof retains only consumers that may be last; singleton release credit can be fixed in advance.
profiles.benefit: Shows how ordering information can replace some dynamic bookkeeping.
profiles.limit: Pegasus reduces cleanup dependencies, not this exact score metadata. Reachability preprocessing is not free.
profiles.match: Closely related prior structural idea, not a verified deployment of this local priority representation.
profiles.input: Preview must precede Filter; both consume Pixels and Alpha.
profiles.output: Filter is the forced last consumer, so release credit does not need those dynamic counters.
profiles.question: Can the required dependency certificate be cheaper than maintaining the original counters?

profiles.title: Delete temporary images only after their final use
profiles.problem: Large image pipelines retain temporary files and can exhaust their working storage.
profiles.role: Cleanup jobs and last-use reasoning release intermediates after all required consumers have finished.
profiles.benefit: The 2007 study evaluates Montage and LIGO, including real execution; Pegasus documents cleanup support.
profiles.limit: Staging, grouped cleanup and parallelism affect results. File bytes are not process RAM.
profiles.match: Real application verified; our one-task-at-a-time replay is not a Montage execution.
profiles.input: Pixels and Alpha must survive until both Preview and Filter finish.
profiles.output: Files are released after their last use; the final exported image is retained.
profiles.question: What does the trace omit, such as temporary files inside a task or data staging?

profiles.title: Assign image-processing tasks to different processors
profiles.product: HEFT-family image and video scheduling research
profiles.problem: A filter runs faster on one processor while another operation favors a different processor.
profiles.role: HEFT combines dependency ranking with estimated finish-time placement on processors.
profiles.benefit: PHEFT evaluates application-shaped LIGO and Montage workloads; embedded scheduling research motivates video and image use.
profiles.limit: PHEFT uses simulated workloads and is a variant. No claim that a named consumer app deploys stock HEFT or that our example measures hardware.
profiles.match: Core HEFT teaching model; application evidence is family-level research.
profiles.input: Decode, Filter, Thumb, Encode and Upload have different costs on two processors.
profiles.output: A dependency-valid processor assignment and a modeled completion time.
profiles.question: Would a better schedule still be worthwhile after the scheduler’s own runtime is counted?

profiles.title: Maintain task order after a small dependency change
profiles.problem: A few affected tasks may lie close together or be spread across a long order interval.
profiles.role: Recover their previous order by sorting affected positions or scanning the interval.
profiles.benefit: Makes the two operation costs visible on the same affected set.
profiles.limit: No verified deployment or originality claim for this exact switch. It is one subroutine, not a complete dynamic sorter.
profiles.match: Inspired by reassignment work in incremental ordering; local mechanism only.
profiles.input: Three affected build tasks are scattered through an eight-task order.
profiles.output: Both procedures recover the same previous relative order.
profiles.question: Can a cheap observable condition choose a method without costing more than the choice saves?

profiles.title: Keep cached data that future tasks will use
profiles.problem: A data-analysis job has limited cache space and may evict data that later tasks need.
profiles.role: LRC uses dependency information rather than recency alone when deciding which cached data to remove.
profiles.benefit: The authors implemented and evaluated a Spark-based prototype; it is not just a hypothetical cache application.
profiles.limit: Not the default policy of all Spark deployments. The demo isolates one count-based eviction, not the full distributed policy.
profiles.match: Core dependency-count motivation; limited eviction demonstration.
profiles.input: Users data has three pending consumers, Products two, Temp one.
profiles.output: The count-based demo selects Temp for eviction.
profiles.question: Is this workload limited by cache misses, or does another cost dominate?

django-media.title: Django form assets — dependency order
django-media.support: Documents why jQuery must precede its dependent scripts and shows merging two asset lists.
django-media.limit: A correctness use case; the page does not report a speedup.

django-code.title: Django Media.merge implementation
django-code.support: The inspected implementation constructs a graph with TopologicalSorter and requests static_order.
django-code.limit: A maintenance branch, not an immutable snapshot. Kahn linkage is through CPython graphlib, not a Django claim of a new sorter.

graphlib.title: Python graphlib — topological task processing
graphlib.support: Tracks unfinished predecessors, releases eligible tasks, and supports concurrent task dispatch.
graphlib.limit: The graph is fixed after preparation. Availability of several tasks is not a guarantee of parallel speedup.

kahn.title: Kahn — Topological Sorting of Large Networks
kahn.limit: Used as an algorithm anchor, not evidence for a modern software speedup.

dask.title: Dask scheduling policy
dask.locator: Last in first out; Break ties with depth-first search
dask.support: Documents a local scheduler policy that favors finishing recently started work.
dask.limit: Do not transfer this policy to every distributed scheduler or infer an optimal memory schedule.

ninja.title: Ninja critical-path priority comparator
ninja.support: Ready-edge comparison uses critical-path weights with an ID tie-break.
ninja.limit: Toy durations in this guide do not reproduce Ninja estimates or a measured build speedup.

ninja-calc.title: Ninja critical-path weight construction
ninja-calc.locator: Plan priority computation; reverse traversal of sorted edges
ninja-calc.support: Computes critical-path weights for build edges.
ninja-calc.limit: Real build scheduling also handles dirty outputs, resource pools and command execution.

lexical.title: NetworkX lexicographical topological sort
lexical.support: Combines dependency validity with a deterministic key order.
lexical.limit: The illustrated asset-manifest use is our adaptation, not a verified named deployment.

generations.title: NetworkX topological generations
generations.support: Partitions a DAG into generations consistent with prerequisites.
generations.limit: A phase-by-phase executor may impose barriers absent from a ready-as-soon-as-possible scheduler.

django-migrate.title: Django migration dependency traversal
django-migrate.support: Uses iterative depth-first search to construct migration plans.
django-migrate.limit: Django traverses parent links for a requested target; our whole-graph DFS demonstration is not a byte-for-byte implementation.

migrations-doc.title: Django migrations — dependencies
migrations-doc.support: Database operations must respect relationships such as a referenced table existing before a foreign key.
migrations-doc.limit: No speedup measurement is stated for DFS itself.

lockdep.title: Linux lock dependency validator
lockdep.support: Detects inconsistent lock acquisition orders that can lead to deadlock.
lockdep.limit: Kernel lock modes and annotations make the actual validation more involved than a plain directed graph.

lockdep-code.title: Linux lockdep breadth-first search
lockdep-code.support: The inspected source uses BFS routines in lock-dependency validation.
lockdep-code.limit: The teaching path is a simplified graph witness, not a kernel trace or a complete lockdep implementation.

tred.title: Graphviz tred — transitive reduction
tred.locator: Transitive reduction filter for directed graphs
tred.support: Provides a concrete graph simplification tool that removes reachability-redundant edges.
tred.limit: Our deployment pipeline is illustrative. Edge labels may encode semantics beyond reachability.

allorders.title: NetworkX all_topological_sorts
allorders.locator: Algorithm reference to Knuth and Szwarcfiter; function output
allorders.limit: Exhaustive checking of tiny fixtures is a local testing application, not a verified large production system.

pk.title: Pearce and Kelly — A Dynamic Topological Sort Algorithm for DAGs
pk.support: Gives the dynamic algorithm and identifies implementations including Abseil.
pk.limit: Reported comparisons are workload-dependent. No universal advantage over recomputation.

abseil.title: Abseil GraphCycles source
abseil.support: Explicitly identifies the Pearce–Kelly algorithm for incremental cycle detection.
abseil.limit: The teaching repair is narrower than the full GraphCycles API and its allocation machinery.

mutex.title: Abseil synchronization guide
mutex.support: Tracks acquired-before lock relationships and reports potential lock-order cycles.
mutex.limit: Detection carries overhead; the guide treats it as a debugging aid, not a proof that a deadlock will occur.

llvm-scc.title: LLVM SCCIterator source
llvm-scc.support: Explicitly names Tarjan DFS for enumerating strongly connected components in linear graph time.
llvm-scc.limit: The sample call graph omits the full compiler IR and pass pipeline.

llvm-pass.title: LLVM new pass manager
llvm-pass.support: Compiler passes can operate on call-graph strongly connected components.
llvm-pass.limit: The existence of this hierarchy is not a claim that every pass uses the identical generic SCCIterator.

heapq.title: Python heapq — changing task priorities
heapq.support: Describes replacement entries and removal markers for changed priorities.
heapq.limit: A version stamp in the teaching engine is an equivalent local technique, not new priority-queue research.

simpy.title: SimPy — time and scheduling
simpy.support: Uses a heap queue of time, event ID and event to process events deterministically.
simpy.limit: The mutable-priority demonstration is not SimPy’s exact event loop.

xla.title: XLA list memory scheduler
xla.support: Uses ready instructions, release-minus-created-byte priorities and unfinished-use counts.
xla.limit: Compiler buffers include aliases and special instruction rules absent from the file model. No new benchmark performed here.

xla-overview.title: OpenXLA — compiler overview
xla-overview.support: XLA compiles machine-learning computations and targets multiple hardware backends.
xla-overview.limit: The JavaScript simulation does not execute a trained model or measure inference speed.

footprint.title: Singh et al. — Optimizing Workflow Data Footprint
footprint.locator: Cleanup dependency reduction; experiments with Montage and LIGO
footprint.support: Studies cleanup placement and dependency reduction on scientific workflows, including real executions.
footprint.limit: Cleanup alone does not resolve the staging behavior of every workflow; changing structure can affect parallelism. Parsed narrative inspected; PDF screenshot retrieval failed in this update.

pegasus.title: Pegasus workflow data management
pegasus.support: Workflow planning can insert cleanup jobs for data no longer needed.
pegasus.limit: Grouped cleanup may delay release. The file-lifetime demo does not implement all Pegasus staging and recovery rules.

montage.title: WfCommons Montage execution instances
montage.support: Provides task dependencies and file metadata for Montage image mosaics.
montage.limit: New interactive inputs are hand-authored teaching examples, not these recorded traces.

heft.title: Topcuoglu, Hariri and Wu — Performance-Effective and Low-Complexity Task Scheduling
heft.locator: HEFT task ranking and processor-selection phases
heft.support: HEFT ranks DAG tasks and chooses processors using estimated finish times.
heft.limit: A heuristic rather than a global optimum; depends on execution and communication estimates.

pheft.title: Drozdov et al. — PHEFT: Pessimistic Image Processing Workflow Scheduling for DSP Clusters
pheft.support: Evaluates scheduling strategies using LIGO- and Montage-shaped workloads and modeled DSP clusters.
pheft.limit: This is a simulation study of a HEFT-family variant, not proof that stock HEFT was deployed in a consumer video app.

arras.title: Arras et al. — List Scheduling in Embedded Systems Under Memory Constraints
arras.support: Studies memory-aware extensions of list scheduling for video decoding and image processing.
arras.limit: Only primary abstract inspected here; numerical or device-specific claims are not reproduced. Online 2014, journal issue 2015.

lrc.title: Yu et al. — LRC: Dependency-Aware Cache Management for Data Analytics Clusters
lrc.support: Uses unfinished-dependent information to improve data caching in the authors’ Spark-based evaluation.
lrc.limit: Not the standard policy of every Spark installation. Benefits depend on cache-sensitive workloads.
